title: Can I get birth control even though I'm a teenager?
content:
Health services for young people are meant to be confidential. The rules on parental consent for under-18s can differ by service, so a health worker can explain what applies to you. Specific service or legal requirements may vary by setting.

Evidence: WHO recommends adolescent SRH services, including contraceptive information and services, without mandatory parental/guardian authorization or notification.

Conditions: Consent wording is interim pending legal review (Children Act 2022 s.16(1)).
source: WHO Recommendations (2018), Ch. 3 §3.3.2, p. 12

title: Do I need my parents' permission to get contraception?
content:
Health services for young people are meant to be confidential. The rules on parental consent for under-18s can differ by service, so a health worker can explain what applies to you.

Evidence: Same as KB-C1.

Conditions: Exact legal age of consent under current Kenyan law not established by available sources — flagged, not stated. Consent wording is interim pending legal review (Children Act 2022 s.16(1)).
source: WHO Recommendations (2018), Ch. 3 §3.3.2, p. 12

title: Which birth control methods can a teenager use?
content:
Kenya's 2025 family planning guideline says adolescents and youth can safely use any contraceptive method that follows the guideline and the medical eligibility criteria. A health worker will help you choose and will explain the possible side effects, because teenagers may find side effects harder to put up with. Using condoms as well gives protection from STIs and HIV.

Evidence: "Adolescents and youth in need of contraceptive services can safely use any method that follows the guideline and MEC criteria." / "Adolescents may be less tolerant of side effects. Healthcare providers shall explain the possible side effects during counselling…" / "Adolescents and youth shall be sensitized on the use of condoms for dual protection against pregnancy and STI/HIV."

Conditions: Medical conditions can change which method suits a girl. No consent rule is stated here (see open issue).

Safety notes: A health worker should confirm the choice, especially if she has a medical condition or might already be pregnant.
source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "FP Services for Adolescents and Youth", p. 25; WHO, Family Planning: A Global Handbook for Providers (2022), Ch. 1, p. 5

title: Do I still need a condom if I'm on the pill or the implant?
content:
Yes, if you want protection from STIs. WHO says condoms are the only contraceptive method that prevents both pregnancy and STIs, including HIV, and Kenya's 2025 guideline says condoms offer dual protection. Other methods prevent pregnancy only, so young people are encouraged to use condoms as well.

Evidence: "Male and female condoms help prevent both pregnancy and most STIs (including HIV)…" / "Therefore, condoms offer dual protection against unintended pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV." / "Adolescents and youth shall be sensitized on the use of condoms for dual protection against pregnancy and STI/HIV." WHO: condoms are the only method that prevents both pregnancy and STIs.

Conditions: Protection depends on using condoms every time and correctly. Step-by-step use is not included (needs the full table on pp. 176 to 178 and a clinician).

Safety notes: If a condom breaks or slips, or she has had unprotected sex, she should see a health worker promptly (see NEW-C-06, on hold). She should also go for any STI symptoms.
source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "Male condom", p. 173 and p. 25; WHO, Family planning/contraception methods fact sheet (3 July 2025)

title: Will contraception make me infertile or stop me having babies later?
content:
No. WHO states that modern contraceptive methods do not cause infertility. Kenya's 2025 guideline says fertility comes back fairly quickly after you stop: on average it can take 3 to 6 months for most methods, and sometimes up to 12 months after the injection (DMPA). If it takes much longer, a health worker can look for other causes.

Evidence: WHO: modern contraceptive methods do not cause infertility. "After stopping a contraceptive, a woman may expect an average of 3 to 6 months delay in returning to fertility for most methods and sometimes up to 12 months for DMPA." / "In cases of prolonged delay in the return to fertility, underlying causes of female sub-fertility or infertility may need to be considered…"

Conditions: The same guideline says return is "immediate" for progestin-only pills (p. 74) and the IUCD (p. 134) and gives other figures for injectables (pp. 96, 108), so no per-method figures are given. Does not cover infertility caused by untreated STIs.

Safety notes: If she is worried about her fertility, or has pelvic pain or unusual discharge, she should see a health worker.
source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "Return to fertility after contraception", p. 31; WHO, Family planning/contraception methods fact sheet (2025); WHO, Family Planning Handbook (2022), Ch. 1, p. 3

title: Is irregular bleeding normal with the implant or the injection?
content:
Light spotting or irregular bleeding is common with both. The guideline says it is common with the injection, especially in the first 6 to 8 months, and with the implant, especially in the first year. It says this is not harmful and usually does not need treatment. If the bleeding keeps going or worries you, see a health worker.

Evidence: Injectables: "Spotting or light bleeding is common during use of injectable contraceptives, particularly during the first 6-8 months of use. It is not harmful. Reassure the client." / "If the bleeding is persistent, assess for gynaecological problems and treat accordingly". Implant: "Reassure client that light bleeding/spotting is common in women using this method especially in the first year. It is not serious and usually does not require treatment." / "If the bleeding is persistent assess for gynaecological problems and treat accordingly".

Conditions: Drug treatments listed in the tables are not included. Heavy bleeding is not covered by these rows.

Safety notes: Persistent or heavy bleeding, pain, or a late period with a possible pregnancy need a health worker.
source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), Table 4.14 (injectables) p. 105; Table 4.20 (implants) p. 117

title: How does the contraceptive implant work, and how long does it last?
content:
The implant is one or two small rods that a trained health worker places under the skin of your upper arm. It slowly releases a hormone that prevents pregnancy. Kenya's 2025 guideline says it is 99.9% effective and starts working 24 hours after it is put in. Depending on the type, it lasts 3 or 5 years. Changes in your bleeding are common, such as spotting or longer or missing periods. It does not protect against STIs, so use condoms too if you are at risk. Only a trained health worker can put it in and take it out.

Evidence: "Implants provide 99.9% effective protection against pregnancy. They are effective 24 hours post insertion." / Table 4.17: Jadelle, 2 rods, 5 years; Implanon and Implanon NXT, 1 rod, 3 years; Levoplant, 2 rods, 3 years. / "The client cannot initiate or discontinue the method on her own as it requires a trained healthcare provider to insert and remove the implant" / "Insertion and removal require minor surgical procedures and may be uncomfortable" / "Change in menstrual pattern including; amenorrhoea, spotting, intermenstrual bleeding or prolonged bleeding." / "Do not protect against STIs, including hepatitis B and HIV. Individuals at risk should use condoms in addition to the implants."

Conditions: Brand names are left out. Some medicines (some HIV medicines, for example) can make implants work less well (p. 109 key messages); not included. Side effects such as headache, nausea and mood changes are not listed. Fertility after removal is not stated because the guideline contradicts itself (see conflicts above).

Safety notes: A health worker must confirm that the implant suits her and that she is not pregnant. Pain, redness or swelling at the arm, or very heavy bleeding, needs a clinic visit (not stated in the pages read; ask the clinician to confirm this line or remove it).
source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "Contraceptive implants", pp. 109 to 110 (Table 4.17 on p. 109)

title: How does the contraceptive injection work, and how often do I need it?
content:
The injection is given by a health worker. The most common kind is given every three months (13 weeks); another kind is given every two months. Kenya's 2025 guideline says it is 99% effective if you get each injection on time, and that the risk of pregnancy is highest when you are late or miss one. Changes in bleeding are common: irregular, heavy or long bleeding, light spotting, or no periods at all. It can take four months or longer for your fertility to return after you stop. It does not protect against STIs, so use condoms too if you are at risk.

Evidence: "Given every three months (13 weeks)" (DMPA) and "Given every two months" (NET-EN), Table 4.11. / "Effectiveness depends on receiving injections on time. Risk of pregnancy is greatest when a woman is late for or misses an injection." / "POIC is 99% effective if used correctly and consistently" / Side effects include "irregular bleeding", "heavy and prolonged bleeding", "light spotting or bleeding", "amenorrhoea, especially after one year of use". / "Return of fertility may be delayed for four months or longer after discontinuation" / "They offer no protection against STIs, including hepatitis B and HIV; individuals at risk for these should use condoms in addition to injectable contraceptives"

Conditions: No age is stated (see conflict 1 above). The self-injected kind (DMPA-SC) is not covered. The grace period for late injections is not given. Return-to-fertility wording matches NEW-C-03; the guideline's own figures vary (pp. 31, 96, 108).

Safety notes: If she is late for an injection and has had unprotected sex, she should see a health worker soon (a held-topic area; do not build more detail without a clinician).
source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "Injectable contraceptives", p. 94 (Table 4.11); p. 95 (effectiveness); p. 96 (limitations and side effects)

title: How does the combined contraceptive pill work, and what are the side effects?
content:
The combined pill has two hormones and is taken once a day, ideally at the same time every day. Kenya's 2025 guideline says it is 99.7% effective if used correctly and consistently. The risk of pregnancy is highest if you start a new pack 3 or more days late or miss 3 or more pills near the start or end of a pack. Mild side effects such as nausea, spotting between periods, headaches, breast tenderness and mood or weight changes are common, especially in the first three months. Severe vomiting or diarrhoea, and some medicines (for example some TB, epilepsy and HIV medicines), can make it work less well, so tell the health worker. The pill does not protect against STIs. If you miss pills, ask a health worker what to do, because it depends on how many you missed and when.

Evidence: "COCs are 99.7% effective in preventing pregnancy if used correctly and consistently." / "The risk of pregnancy is greatest when a woman starts a new pill pack 3 or more days late, or misses 3 or more pills near the beginning or the end of a pill pack." / "COCs must be taken daily to be effective, preferably at the same time each day." / "Contraceptive effectiveness could also be lowered in the presence of gastroenteritis, severe vomiting, and diarrhoea." / "Effectiveness may be lowered if the client is on anti-TB drugs" / "Nausea (more common in the first three months)" / "COCs do not offer protection against STls, including hepatitis B and HIV." / MEC Category 1: "Age: from menarche to 40 years"

Conditions: Missed-pill instructions are conditional tables (Table 4.4, p. 72) and are not summarised here (see appendix to `kb-candidates-2025-fp-guideline.md`). Serious but rare side effects (blood clots, stroke) are listed on p. 60 and are not included without a clinician. The pill does not suit everyone (medical conditions change eligibility).

Safety notes: A health worker should check that the pill is suitable. Severe chest pain, a very bad headache, or a swollen painful leg need urgent care (not stated in the pages read; the clinician should decide whether to add warning signs).
source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "Combined Oral Contraceptive (COCs) Pills", p. 58 (what it is); p. 59 (effectiveness, first limitations); p. 60 (limitations, side effects); p. 61 (eligibility)

title: I might have been exposed to HIV. Is there something I can take to stop it?
content:
Yes — post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is a course of medication started as soon as possible after exposure. Both Kenyan and WHO guidance agree it should be started within 72 hours, since it becomes less effective the longer you wait.

Evidence: PEP (28-day ARV regimen) must be initiated within 72 hours of exposure per both sources — this is one of the few points of full agreement between MoH and WHO.

Conditions: Specific drug names/dosing not established by sources — do not include in the answer.

Safety notes: Must direct to immediate facility-based care — this is time-critical.
source: Kenya MoH YFS Guidelines (2005), Annex 1, pp. 26–28 and WHO (2018), Ch. 7 §7.3.5/7.3.14, pp. 43, 46

title: I have unusual discharge, itching, burning or lower belly pain. Could it be an STI?
content:
It could be, but unusual discharge can have other causes too, and only a test can tell which. Many STIs cause no symptoms at all. Kenya's 2026 guidelines now prefer lab tests that find the exact infection before treatment, so ask for a test at a health facility. Lower belly pain, pain during sex or bleeding between periods needs a visit soon, because untreated infections can spread to the womb and tubes.

Evidence: Laboratory-confirmed (aetiological) diagnosis is the preferred approach to STI care in Kenya. Chlamydia symptoms in women include abnormal vaginal discharge, pain on passing urine, and bleeding after sex or between periods; gonorrhoea in women may cause abnormal discharge and lower abdominal discomfort. Untreated infection can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy and infertility.

Conditions: Where a facility has no laboratory, the guideline still allows clinical diagnosis (s. 3.3.2 p. 162). No treatment or drug advice is given. The 2018 guideline (the earlier source) was replaced by the 2026 edition; the privacy sentence that came from it is dropped.

Safety notes: Lower belly pain with fever, or pain during sex, needs a clinic visit soon. She should not self-treat.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.3.1 p. 161; s. 3.5.1 Chlamydia p. 171; s. 3.5.2 Gonorrhoea p. 171; WHO, Sexually transmitted infections fact sheet

title: Can STIs be cured, and can they harm me if I leave them?
content:
Four common STIs (syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis) can be cured with antibiotics. HIV and herpes cannot be cured, but medicine can keep them under control. Some untreated infections can spread and cause pelvic inflammatory disease, so it is better to get tested and treated early.

Evidence: WHO: syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis are curable; HIV and herpes are not but can be managed. Kenya 2026: untreated chlamydia and gonorrhoea can ascend to cause PID, ectopic pregnancy and infertility; testing finds the exact infection.

Conditions: The curable and not-curable statements rest on the WHO fact sheet only; IG2026 pages read do not state curability. Being cured does not protect against catching the infection again. Partner treatment is not included. The 2018 guideline citation is dropped.

Safety notes: She should go to a clinic for testing and treatment rather than self-treating.
source: WHO, Sexually transmitted infections fact sheet; Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.3.1 p. 161; s. 3.5.1 and 3.5.2 p. 171

title: Is the HPV vaccine available to me, and am I old enough?
content:
Kenya's 2026 HIV and STI guideline says the HPV vaccine is available in Kenya for girls aged 9 to 14, and since November 2025 it is given as a single dose. If you are older than that, ask at a government health facility whether you can still get it.

Evidence: Kenya's HPV programme targets 10-year-old girls and moved from a two-dose to a single-dose schedule in November 2025. IG2026 (p. 182) adds that the HPV vaccine is highly effective for preventing genital warts, but does not state who is eligible.

Conditions: Sources disagree on the target age (WHO AFRO: 10-year-olds; news reports: 10 to 14). Whether it is free and whether catch-up is offered for older girls is not stated in any primary source seen, including IG2026 and FP7.

Safety notes: Do not tell a girl over 14 she is ineligible. She should ask at a clinic.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 1.5.2.5, p. 57; WHO AFRO, Kenya transitions to single-dose HPV vaccination schedule (page dated 1 November 2025)

title: Can I take PrEP to prevent HIV? I'm a teenager.
content:
PrEP is medicine that HIV-negative people can use to lower their risk of getting HIV. Kenya's 2026 guidelines say it is not for adolescents under 15. From age 15, a health worker can check whether it suits you. You need an HIV test first. There are now several forms, including a daily pill, a vaginal ring, and injections given every 2 or every 6 months, and a health worker will help you choose. Ask about condoms too, because PrEP does not protect against other STIs.

Evidence: PrEP is indicated for HIV-negative people at ongoing risk; "Adolescents under 15 years" is listed as a contraindication; eligibility requires a confirmed HIV-negative test; options are daily oral PrEP, the dapivirine vaginal ring (every 28 days), cabotegravir long-acting injection (every 8 weeks) and lenacapavir injection (every 26 weeks).

Conditions: Not every facility offers every form. Some forms have extra conditions (kidney or liver checks). The pages read do not state the consent rule for 15- to 17-year-olds (Table 1.12 p. 17 says "national consent guidance"). "PrEP does not protect against other STIs" is not stated on the pages read; keep the WHO citation or remove the sentence.

Safety notes: Girls under 15 who are at risk should go to a clinic or youth-friendly service for other prevention options. If she may have been exposed in the last 3 days she needs PEP urgently, not PrEP.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 1.3.1 pp. 17 to 18; s. 1.3.3 p. 19; Table 1.15 p. 21; WHO, HIV fact sheet

title: Can I have an STI without knowing?
content:
Yes. Many STIs cause no symptoms. For example, chlamydia causes no symptoms in about 7 in 10 women, and gonorrhoea is also often symptom-free in women. If they are not treated, they can spread to the womb and tubes and later cause pain, a pregnancy outside the womb, or trouble getting pregnant. The only way to know is a test at a health facility.

Evidence: Genital chlamydia infection is asymptomatic in about 70% of women; gonorrhoea is often asymptomatic in women (fewer than half of infected women report symptoms); untreated infections may cause PID, ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility; laboratory testing also detects asymptomatic infection.

Conditions: The 70% figure is the guideline's figure for chlamydia in women. It is not given for other STIs. Not every untreated infection causes complications.

Safety notes: Anyone who has had sex without a condom, or whose partner may have an STI, can ask for a test at a clinic. She does not have to have symptoms.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.5.1 p. 171; s. 3.5.2 p. 171; s. 3.3.1 p. 161

title: If a person with HIV takes their medicine, can they still pass HIV to a partner during sex?
content:
Not if their viral load stays undetectable. Kenya's 2026 guidelines say that people whose blood tests show an undetectable viral load on two tests six months apart have effectively no risk of passing HIV on through sex. This is called U=U: undetectable equals untransmittable. It depends on carrying on with the medicine and the clinic's viral load tests. It does not apply in pregnancy and breastfeeding, to injecting drug use, or to needle-stick injuries.

Evidence: Definition: a durable undetectable viral load (two consecutive results below 200 copies/ml six months apart) means effectively no risk of sexual transmission. U=U messaging is not applicable in pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV, people who inject drugs, or needle-stick injuries.

Conditions: This is about HIV only; it says nothing about other STIs. A person cannot tell her partner's viral load without the partner's own results.

Safety notes: A partner of someone with HIV can ask a clinic about testing and prevention (PrEP or PEP). For other STIs, a test is still the only way to know.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 1.6.5 p. 97

title: Is vaginal discharge always a sign of an STI?
content:
No. Bacterial vaginosis, the most common cause of vaginal discharge in women of childbearing age, is not an STI, and neither is a yeast infection (thrush). Trichomoniasis is an STI that can cause a yellow or greenish, sometimes frothy, discharge and itching, and many women who have it have no symptoms. Because these can look alike, you can't tell by yourself. A health worker can test you and tell you which it is.

Evidence: BV is the most common cause of vaginal discharge in women of childbearing age and is not an STI. Candidiasis is not an STI. About 50 to 85% of women with T. vaginalis may have no symptoms; symptomatic women usually have abnormal discharge, and about half have vulval itching, with a yellow or greenish, sometimes frothy discharge.

Conditions: No description of normal discharge is given because none was found in the pages read. No treatments are given. This overlaps with the "discharge" gap topic, so the gynaecologist should approve it as the answer or replace it.

Safety notes: Lower belly pain, fever or pain during sex needs a visit soon. A girl who may be pregnant should be seen before taking any treatment.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.5.4 p. 172; s. 3.5.5 p. 172; s. 3.5.6 p. 173

title: How do I get tested for HIV, and can I test myself?
content:
You can be tested at a health facility, and a health worker should ask for your consent first. Kenya's guidelines also approve HIV self-test kits, where you collect your own sample (from your mouth or a drop of blood) and read the result yourself. A self-test that shows a reactive result must be confirmed at a health facility with the national tests. If you test negative, a health worker can talk to you about ways to stay protected.

Evidence: HIV testing is offered with informed consent. HIV self-testing uses Ministry of Health-approved kits (oral or blood-based) and is particularly effective for reaching adolescents; a reactive self-test must be confirmed through the national testing algorithm. HIV-negative clients are linked to prevention services.

Conditions: The pages read do not state where to buy self-test kits, what they cost, or any age limit; no cost or "free" claim is made. A recent exposure can be missed by an early test (see NEW-S-10).

Safety notes: If a self-test is reactive, she should go to a facility for confirmation and support, not decide on her own. A recent exposure within 72 hours needs PEP urgently (see NEW-S-06).
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 1.1.1 p. 1; s. 1.1.3 p. 2

title: How soon after sex can an HIV test tell me if I have HIV?
content:
Not straight away. After HIV gets into the body there is a "window period" before a test can detect it, and different tests detect it at different times, so an early negative result may not be reliable. A health worker will tell you when to test again. If a result is unclear, Kenya's guidelines say to test again after 14 days. After a possible exposure, check-up tests are repeated at 28 days and at 12 weeks.

Evidence: The window period is the time between exposure and detectable antibodies; different tests detect at different stages. Inconclusive results are retested after 14 days. After PEP, HIV testing is repeated at 28 days and 12 weeks; blood or organ donation is avoided until confirmed HIV-negative at 12 weeks.

Conditions: No single number of days is given for when a test becomes reliable. The 28-day and 12-week schedule is the PEP follow-up schedule, not a general rule for all tests.

Safety notes: A possible exposure within the last 3 days is urgent: go to a facility about PEP (see NEW-S-06). Use condoms until the result is confirmed.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 1.1.7 Table 1.6 p. 12; s. 1.2.4 p. 16; s. 1.2.5 p. 16

title: What is pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)?
content:
PID is an infection of the womb, tubes and the area around them. It is usually caused by STIs that were not treated, such as chlamydia and gonorrhoea. The signs can be mild or missing, so it is often missed. Pelvic or lower belly pain is the main sign, and fever or unusual discharge can come with it. Treatment that is delayed can leave lasting damage to the tubes and make it harder to get pregnant. See a health worker soon if you have lower belly pain, and go to hospital urgently for severe pelvic pain or a high fever.

Evidence: PID is an inflammatory disorder of the upper genital tract commonly caused by untreated chlamydia, gonorrhoea, trichomonas and Mycoplasma genitalium; symptoms can be subtle or absent; delay contributes to complications; diagnosis is based on pelvic or abdominal pain with tenderness, and fever and purulent discharge add to the picture; severe pelvic pain or high fever (above 38 degrees) are criteria for hospital referral. Complications include ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility.

Conditions: Treatment details are not included. The referral list in the guideline is for clinicians; the "go to hospital urgently" wording here is a simplified version for lay readers.

Safety notes: Severe pelvic pain can also be an ectopic pregnancy or appendicitis, so it should never be treated at home.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.6 pp. 178-179; s. 3.5.1 p. 171

title: What are genital warts, and can I prevent them?
content:
Genital warts are small growths on or around the genitals or the anus, caused mostly by two types of HPV (types 6 and 11). Some are visible and some are inside the vagina or anus. They can pass to a partner, and condoms help reduce the spread. A health worker should look at any new growth, because other conditions can look similar. The HPV vaccine is very effective at preventing genital warts. HPV that causes no signs usually clears by itself.

Evidence: Anogenital warts are largely caused by HPV genotypes 6 and 11; may be internal; highly infectious to partners, and condoms help reduce transmission; examination is needed to rule out other causes; subclinical genital HPV infection typically clears spontaneously; the quadrivalent or nonavalent HPV vaccine is highly effective for preventing anogenital warts.

Conditions: No treatments are given. Whether and where a girl can get the vaccine is not stated here (see NEW-S-03, still unverified).

Safety notes: She should see a health worker for any growth rather than trying home treatments.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.9 p. 182

title: I have painful sores or blisters on my genitals. Could it be herpes or syphilis?
content:
It could be. Painful blisters or sores, with itching or burning when you pass urine, can be genital herpes, which can come back. Syphilis and other infections can also cause genital sores, and sometimes more than one infection is present. Some sores are not from STIs at all, for example a yeast infection or an injury. A health worker can test you and tell you which it is, so go to a clinic rather than treating it yourself.

Evidence: Genital ulcers can have more than one infectious cause (for example herpes and syphilis); genital herpes presents with painful vesicles or ulcers, itching, burning, dysuria and recurrent outbreaks; some genital lesions are not sexually transmitted (yeast, trauma and others); diagnosis uses tests such as PCR.

Conditions: No treatments or doses are given. Whether herpes can be cured is not stated in the pages read, so the answer does not say.

Safety notes: Sores plus fever, or large painful swellings in the groin, need a visit soon.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.4 and Table 3.8 p. 164

title: I have itching in my pubic hair or private area. Could it be lice or scabies?
content:
It could be. Pubic lice are tiny insects that live in pubic hair and usually pass on through sexual contact. A health worker can see the lice and their eggs on the hair. Scabies is a skin condition caused by tiny mites that makes the skin very itchy. In adults it is often caught through sex, but this is not always so. Itching can also have other causes, such as thrush. Both lice and scabies can be treated, so see a health worker rather than guessing.

Evidence: "Pediculosis pubis is caused by the parasite Phthirus pubis and is usually transmitted by sexual contact" / "The clinical diagnosis is based on typical symptoms of itching in the pubic region, lice and nits can be observed on pubic hair." / "Scabies is a skin infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, which causes pruritus." / "Scabies among adults is frequently sexually acquired, although scabies among children usually is not."

Conditions: The guideline lists treatments (creams, lotions, tablets); none are named. "Thrush" and other causes of itching come from IG2026 s. 3.5.6 (p. 173), where candidiasis is described as "not an STI" (see NEW-S-08). Do not tell a girl that scabies means she has had sex: among children it usually is not sexually acquired.

Safety notes: If itching is with sores, unusual discharge or pain, she should see a health worker. If she says she was forced, route to the existing help reply (not a topic for this entry).
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.10.1 Pediculosis Pubis, p. 184; s. 3.10.2 Scabies, p. 185

title: Can I catch hepatitis B from sex, and how can I prevent it?
content:
Hepatitis B is a virus that harms the liver. Kenya's 2026 guideline says it spreads through contact with infected blood or other body fluids, mainly through sex, sharing needles, needle-stick injuries, and from an infected mother to her baby at birth. Vaccination is the main way to prevent it, along with safe healthcare practices. Signs can include yellow skin or eyes, dark urine and tiredness. Ask a health worker whether you are vaccinated and whether you should be tested.

Evidence: "Hepatitis B is transmitted horizontally through exposures to infected blood or other body fluids, primarily via sexual contact, sharing needles, occupational exposure (like needle stick injuries), and vertically from an infected mother to her infant during birth." / Prevention: "Hepatitis B birth dose and routine immunization" (Table 4.2). / Features: "Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)", "Dark-coloured urine", fatigue. / FP7 p. 110: contraceptives "Do not protect against STIs, including hepatitis B and HIV. Individuals at risk should use condoms".

Conditions: The pages read do not give the vaccine schedule or catch-up rules for adolescents, so none is stated. IG2026 p. 57 says the hepatitis B vaccine is for "newborns and high-risk groups" (in a section on people living with HIV); whether a teenager is eligible needs a clinician. Hepatitis A, C and E are not covered.

Safety notes: Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or stomach pain need a health worker soon. She should not assume she is protected.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 4.6.2 p. 192; s. 4.4 Table 4.2 and s. 4.5 p. 189; Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), p. 110

title: Could a painless sore or a rash on my palms be syphilis?
content:
It could. Kenya's 2026 guideline says early syphilis causes a painless sore, usually at the place where the infection got in (the genitals, anus or mouth), about 3 weeks after exposure. Because it does not hurt, it can be missed. Weeks later, about 6 to 8 weeks after the sore, it can cause a skin rash, especially on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Syphilis can be found with a blood test and cured with antibiotics, so see a health worker rather than waiting for it to go away.

Evidence: Primary syphilis (table cells, read as fragments): "Painless chancre at" / "site of inoculation" (genital, anal, or oral) / "~3 weeks after" exposure. Secondary syphilis: "Skin rash, especially" / "on palms and soles" / "~6-8 weeks after". Diagnosis by serological testing (RPR/VDRL, then a treponemal test). WHO: syphilis is curable.

Conditions: Treatment drugs are not named. The guideline's blood-test details are not explained. Other conditions cause sores (herpes, yeast, injury; s. 3.4 p. 164, see NEW-S-13), so a sore does not by itself mean syphilis. "Curable" rests on WHO, as in NEW-S-02.

Safety notes: Syphilis in pregnancy affects the baby (not covered here); a pregnant girl with a sore should see a health worker without delay.
source: Kenya MoH/NASCOP, Integrated Guidelines (2026), s. 3.4 Table 3.8, p. 166 (primary) and p. 167 (secondary); WHO, Sexually transmitted infections fact sheet

title: Do I have to get a pelvic exam right away at my first visit?
content:
No — youth-friendly facilities should let you delay pelvic exams and blood tests until you're ready, while still addressing your immediate needs another way.

Evidence: YFS facilities must offer options to delay pelvic exams and blood tests until the client is psychologically/emotionally prepared, alongside alternative ways to meet immediate needs.

Conditions: 2005 document — flag for domain expert to confirm still standard practice.
source: Kenya MoH YFS Guidelines (2005), Ch. 3 §3.3, p. 18

title: Can I stay in school if I'm pregnant, and can I go back after the baby?
content:
Under Kenya's 2020 national school re-entry guidelines, a pregnant learner is allowed to stay in school for as long as possible and to sit national exams if her health allows. After delivery she is re-admitted to the same class she was in before. The guidelines give the return time as six months after delivery and also as the start of the next calendar year, so ask your school's guidance and counselling teacher what applies to you.

Evidence: A pregnant learner shall be allowed to remain in school as long as possible and to sit national exams if her health permits; after delivery she is re-admitted to the same class unconditionally.

Conditions: The guidelines state the return both as six months after delivery and as the start of the next calendar year, which can differ. These are national guidelines; practice in schools varies.

Safety notes: If a school refuses, she can ask the guidance and counselling teacher. A verified escalation route was not found.
source: Ministry of Education, Kenya, National Guidelines for School Re-Entry in Early Learning and Basic Education (2020), Section 3.2

title: What warning signs in pregnancy mean I should go to hospital right away?
content:
Kenya's Mother and Child Health Handbook lists these warning signs: vaginal bleeding, severe stomach pain, the baby moving less or not at all, fits, fever, a severe headache, waters breaking, and swelling of the face and hands. If you have any of them, go to a health facility straight away.

Evidence: The handbook lists these danger signs and advises being prepared to seek skilled care at a health facility for any of them.

Conditions: A lay list from the handbook, not a clinical triage protocol. An earlier (2016) copy lists a different set of signs, so use the 2020 edition.

Safety notes: Any of these signs means going to the nearest health facility immediately. She should not wait or treat at home.
source: Kenya MoH, Mother & Child Health Handbook (Afya ya Mama na Mtoto), revised 2020

title: Do I need iron and folic acid tablets in pregnancy, and what should I eat?
content:
Kenya's Mother and Child Health Handbook says to take iron and folic acid supplements every day throughout pregnancy and to eat at least 5 of the 10 food groups each day. The clinic gives you the tablets. If you feel very tired, look pale or get breathless, tell the clinic.

Evidence: Take iron and folic acid supplements every day throughout pregnancy and eat at least 5 of the 10 food groups every day.

Conditions: The dose is for clinicians to prescribe and is not given here. Side effects were not found in a source. The WHO iron and folic acid guideline (2012) could not be opened.

Safety notes: Tiredness with a pale look or breathlessness may be anaemia and needs a clinic visit.
source: Kenya MoH, Mother & Child Health Handbook (2020); Kenya MoH, Basic Obstetric Protocols, 1st ed. (2026)

title: How can I know if I am pregnant or not, and how do I get a pregnancy test?
content:
The way to find out is a urine pregnancy test. Kenya's guidelines say that when a period is late, irregular or you are not sure, a urine pregnancy test should be done. Ask a health worker or a youth-friendly clinic for one. Until you have a test result, you cannot be sure you are not pregnant. Use a condom or avoid sex until your period comes or the result is confirmed.

Evidence: "if uncertain, irregular, or delayed then a urine pregnancy test should be performed" (IG2026, p. 29). "If pregnancy testing is not available, counsel the client to use barrier methods or abstain from intercourse until her menses occur or pregnancy is confirmed" (FP7, p. 45). "Pregnancy cannot completely be ruled out using the checklist" (FP7, p. 45).

Conditions: Both sources are written for health workers, not for girls. Neither says how soon after sex or a missed period is a test reliable, so no timing is given. The line "ask a health worker or a youth-friendly clinic for one" is not stated in these pages; it is a referral note for the clinician to confirm. FP7 p. 45 lists situations where a provider can be reasonably sure a client is not pregnant (for example a negative test and no unprotected sex in 3 weeks). That is a provider screening tool and is deliberately NOT turned into advice to the girl.

Safety notes: Never tell her she is not pregnant. If she may have been raped or forced, route to the help reply (1195, 999, 112). Possible pregnancy with severe pain or heavy bleeding needs a facility visit. Held-topic group C should still send late-period and "am I pregnant" queries to a health worker; this entry would answer the "how do I get a test" wording only if the clinicians and Mr. Ouma agree it should replace or sit beside the held reply.
source: Kenya MoH, HIV/STI Guidelines (IG2026), p. 29; Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guidelines for Health Service Providers, 7th ed. (FP7), p. 45. Both quotes were found by exact text search; page numbers are printed pages and should be re-checked in the PDFs.

title: Will the clinic tell my parents what I talked to them about?
content:
Youth-friendly health services are expected to keep what you share confidential, including from parents — except in specific situations where the law requires disclosure, which staff should explain to you clearly.

Evidence: Providers must maintain confidentiality and not leak information to parents; legal exceptions exist but aren't specified in this source.

Conditions: Exact legal exceptions not established by this source — flag if a user's question implies a specific legal scenario.
source: Kenya MoH YFS Guidelines (2005), Ch. 3 §3.2–3.3, pp. 16–17

title: What age counts as "youth" or "adolescent" for these services?
content:
Kenyan services define adolescents as 10–19, youth as 15–24, and young people as 10–24 — these terms are often used interchangeably.

Evidence: Age range definitions for target populations in Kenya.
source: Kenya MoH YFS Guidelines (2005), Ch. 1 §1.1.2, p. 2

title: Is my period normal, and when should I see a health worker?
content:
Periods vary from girl to girl. Kenya's school handbook says some girls have cycles of 21 days and others 35 days, and bleeding usually lasts 2 to 7 days, with about 5 days the average. In the first years after periods start they may not be regular. WHO says bleeding that is unpredictable, infrequent, very painful or heavy, or that stops you doing normal activities, could point to an underlying health condition, so see a health worker. A late period can have many causes, including pregnancy.

Evidence: MHM: "Some girls menstruate every 28 days while others have longer cycles of 35 days or shorter cycles of 21 days." / "Menstruation usually last from 2-7 days with 5 days being the average length of menstrual flow." / "Menstrual cycle for the first few years is not regular for some girls." WHO: menstrual bleeding that is unpredictable, infrequent, very painful, heavy, or disrupts normal activities could suggest an underlying health condition.

Conditions: The handbook does not say when bleeding is too heavy or too long, or how many days late a period must be before testing. Confirm the handbook's edition and date (cover says 2020; file name says April 2022).

Safety notes: Very heavy bleeding, or pain that stops usual activities, needs a facility visit. A late period should be routed to a health worker or a pregnancy test, not diagnosed (held-topic group C).
source: Kenya MoH and MoE, Menstrual Hygiene Management in Schools: A Handbook for Teachers, "Facts about Menstruation", p. 10; WHO, Menstrual health fact sheet

title: What can I do about period pain?
content:
Many girls have period pain: WHO says more than 2 in 3 women and girls do. Kenya's school handbook suggests putting a bottle of hot water on your tummy, doing some exercise such as skipping or swimming, drinking plenty of water and eating a healthy, balanced diet. If you want a painkiller, ask a pharmacist or health worker which one is safe for you. See a health worker if the pain goes on for a long time or stops your usual activities.

Evidence: MHM: "Place hot water in a bottle on the abdomen to relieve cramps." / "Physical exercises such as swimming, running, jogging, skipping, hula hoop." / "Eat healthy balanced diet all the time." / "Drink plenty of water." / "Please visit a doctor if you are experiencing discomforts for a longer period of time." WHO: more than 2 out of 3 women and girls have pain with menstrual bleeding. NHS: see a GP if pain stops usual daily activities.

Conditions: The handbook gives no painkiller advice; the painkiller line rests on the NHS source from the 6 Oct draft. No doses. Some painkillers are unsuitable for some people (for example with stomach ulcers or asthma), which was not verified here.

Safety notes: Severe or worsening pelvic pain needs a facility visit. Pain with a late period could be pregnancy-related, so it should not be called just a period.
source: Kenya MoH and MoE, MHM Handbook for Teachers, "Pain Management of Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS)", p. 20; WHO, Menstrual health fact sheet; NHS, Period pain (UK)

title: How do I manage my period hygienically?
content:
Kenya's school handbook gives these tips: change your pad or other menstrual product regularly, wash your hands with soap and clean water before and after changing it, bathe or shower at least once a day, and change your underwear every day or when it is soiled. Wash the outside of the vagina with water only, and do not put soap, deodorant or liquids inside the vagina. Wipe from front to back after using the toilet.

Evidence: "Taking a bath or shower at least once a day." / "Using of a clean undergarment and changing them regularly, a minimum of every day or when soiled." / "Changing of menstrual product and material regularly during menstruation." / "Ensuring hand washing with soap and clean water before and after changing the product." / "Washing the vagina with water only! … the vagina has its own self-cleaning mechanism. An external cleaning agent or deodorant should not be used and too much soap can cause itching." / "Wiping from front to back following urination or defecation to avoid infections." / "Avoiding douching…" / "Infrequent change of menstrual products can cause urinary tract infections (UTIs) and reproductive tract infections (RTIs)."

Conditions: The handbook gives no number of hours between changes. Tampon and cup advice, including toxic shock syndrome (pp. 19 to 20), is not included without a clinician.

Safety notes: Unusual discharge, itching or burning should be seen at a clinic. Toxic shock signs (sudden high fever, rash, vomiting, confusion) are an emergency but the source puts them under tampon use, so they are held out of this entry.
source: Kenya MoH and MoE, MHM Handbook for Teachers, "Safe and Hygiene Practices During Menstruation", p. 21; pp. 19 to 20; Kenya MoH, Menstrual Hygiene Management Policy 2019 to 2030

title: What changes happen to my body at puberty, and when does my first period come?
content:
The first sign of puberty in most girls is breast 'buds', followed by body hair and a growth spurt. Kenya's school handbook says a girl's first period happens between the ages of 9 and 17, and some girls get theirs as early as 9. Periods may be irregular for the first few years. Timing varies from girl to girl, so if you are worried about your development, talk to a health worker.

Evidence: AAP: breast buds are the earliest sign of puberty. MHM: the first period occurs "between 9-17 years"; "Some girls have their first menstruation as early as nine years of age."; "Menstrual cycle for the first few years is not regular for some girls."

Conditions: The handbook's own diagram on p. 8 says an egg matures "between the ages of 8 and 19 years"; the 9 to 17 range is used. The AAP source is American. KDHS 2022 was not opened.

Safety notes: If there are no signs of puberty, or no period well past the usual ages, talk to a health worker. No verified age thresholds for worry were found.
source: Kenya MoH and MoE, MHM Handbook for Teachers, "Menstruation and Semenarche" p. 8 and "Facts about Menstruation" p. 10; American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org, Physical Development in Girls (2019)

title: What does a youth-friendly health service offer, and what should I expect?
content:
Kenya's 2025 family planning guideline says services for adolescents and youth should be equitable, accessible, acceptable, appropriate and effective. In practice that means services should be affordable, open at convenient times such as after school and on weekends, give you information you can understand, and keep what you say confidential, including when you register and in your records. You should be able to speak to a provider in a place where no one can see or hear you.

Evidence: "Healthcare providers … shall provide adolescent and youth-friendly services that are equitable, accessible, acceptable, appropriate and effective…" / "SRH services must be affordable and available to all adolescents and youth." / "…made obtainable during convenient hours, including after school or work and during weekends and holidays…" / "Confidentiality should be maintained at all times, including during registration, consultation, record-keeping and disclosure." / "The point of service delivery should be located in a place that affords auditory and visual privacy." / "The services should offer appropriate information that will be understood by the client…"

Conditions: These are standards for how services should be delivered; a given facility may not meet them. The pages describe family planning services; they do not list a full package of services, facility types or helplines, so none is named. The 2005 and 2016 YFS guidelines are not used. The same section (p. 25) says adolescents under 18 give assent and a guardian gives consent for FP services; this entry does not state a consent rule.

Safety notes: Urgent symptoms (heavy bleeding, severe pain, possible pregnancy) need prompt care.
source: Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guideline, 7th ed. (2025), "FP Services for Adolescents and Youth", p. 23; Table 3.3 "Principles for the provision of adolescent and youth-responsive services", p. 24

title: Why do I feel tired, moody or get pimples before my period?
content:
That could be premenstrual syndrome (PMS), a group of symptoms linked to your cycle that start 1 to 2 weeks before your period. Kenya's school handbook lists tender breasts, pimples, tiredness, trouble sleeping, headache or backache, bloating, changes in appetite, and mood swings or feeling tearful. For some girls PMS is just a monthly bother, and for others it is so strong that it is hard to get through the day. It goes away when your periods stop, for example during pregnancy. If it is making daily life hard, or you feel very sad or anxious, see a health worker.

Evidence: "PMS symptoms occur 1 to 2 weeks before your menstruation or monthly bleeding starts." / "For some people, PMS is just a monthly bother. For others, it may be so severe that it makes it hard to even get through the day." / Symptoms listed: "Acne/pimples", "Swollen or tender breasts", "Feeling tired", "Trouble sleeping", "Headache or backache", "Tension, irritability, mood swings, or crying spells", "Anxiety or depression". / "PMS goes away when your monthly periods stop, such as when you get pregnant or go through menopause."

Conditions: The handbook does not say what counts as severe or when to see a health worker for PMS (the "visit a doctor" tip on p. 20 is about long-lasting discomfort). Late-period and pregnancy questions go to the held-topic rules. See NEW-G-02 for cramps.

Safety notes: Persistent low mood or anxiety that does not go away needs a health worker or counsellor. If she says she wants to harm herself, the Safety Net reply applies, not this entry.
source: Kenya MoH and MoE, MHM in Schools: A Handbook for Teachers, "Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS)", p. 9; "Pain Management of Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS)", p. 20

title: What can I use during my period: pads, tampons or a cup?
content:
Kenya's school handbook lists four choices: disposable pads, reusable pads, tampons and menstrual cups. The choice depends on what you prefer, whether you have water and a place to dispose of products, and what suits your underwear. Disposable pads are easy to use but cost more and are not always available. Reusable pads cost less but need water and somewhere private to wash and dry them; if they are not cleaned well they can cause infections, and you should not share them. Tampons and cups go inside the vagina, and need instructions before you use them. A tampon left in too long can cause a serious illness called toxic shock syndrome, so change it often. Keep products in a clean, cool, dry place.

Evidence: "Existing products and materials include disposable and reusable sanitary pads, tampons, and reusable menstrual cups." / "The choice between reusable and disposable products depends predominantly on:" "One's choice", "Availability of disposal and water facilities", "The compatibility with girl's and women's preferred undergarments." / Disposable pads: "Not easily available in rural areas", "Relatively costly". / Reusable pads: "Requires access to water", "for washing the pad", "Need for somewhere" / "private to wash and dry", "If not hygienically" / "cleaned it can predispose" / "including candidasis", "not to share". / Tampons: "Requires instruction before use"; "If hygiene and frequent changing of tampons is not maintained can lead to Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)". / Cups: "Requires instructions before use". / "Menstrual products and materials should be stored in a clean, cool and dry place that is free from dust, smoke and chemicals"

Conditions: The handbook says some cultures and religions do not accept tampons or cups; not included. It gives no number of hours between changes (see NEW-G-03). It is a teacher's handbook, not clinical guidance. Toxic shock signs are not listed in the pages used.

Safety notes: Sudden high fever, rash, vomiting or feeling very unwell while using a tampon is an emergency (not stated in the pages read; the clinician should confirm adding this).
source: Kenya MoH and MoE, MHM in Schools: A Handbook for Teachers, "Menstrual Products", pp. 14 to 16 (choice p. 14; storage tip and table pp. 15 to 16)

title: How do I dispose of a used pad safely?
content:
Kenya's school handbook says to wrap the used pad in paper, put it in a dustbin and close the lid. Keep period waste separate from other rubbish by using a sanitary bin where there is one. Throwing pads in pit latrines or toilets is shown as the wrong way, because it blocks drains and can pollute water.

Evidence: Figure 1, "Proper storage of menstrual waste": "Wrap in paper", "Put in dustbin", "Close the lid". / "Girls and women should separate menstrual waste from the general waste by explicitly disposing of the menstrual waste in designated sanitary bins." / "In the absence of bins, awareness should be raised on how to safely and hygienically handle used disposable sanitary pads." / The handbook's "Improper Ways of Disposing Menstrual Waste" figure shows "Pit latrines" (with pour-flush and western toilets). / Harms of improper disposal include "Clogging of drainage system.", water contamination, and "Scavenging poses the risk of contracting diseases from infected menstrual waste."

Conditions: The last sentence ("keep it until you can dispose of it safely") is not stated in the handbook; the clinician or Mr. Ouma should keep it or remove it. Incineration and community collection are not included. The "improper ways" labels come from a figure caption, so confirm them against the printed page.
source: Kenya MoH and MoE, MHM in Schools: A Handbook for Teachers, "Safe Disposal of Used Menstrual Products", pp. 24 to 25

title: What is a period, and why does it happen?
content:
A period is a regular discharge of blood and tissue from the lining of the womb (uterus), which comes out through the vagina. Kenya's school handbook explains it like this: usually one egg matures in each cycle and travels from the ovary down the fallopian tube, and meanwhile the womb lining gets thicker. If the egg is not fertilised, the body sheds the lining as blood, and that is your period. If the egg is fertilised, the lining provides a home for a growing baby. A period is a normal part of growing up. It starts at puberty and stops later in life at menopause.

Evidence: "Menstruation is a regular discharge of blood and tissue from inner lining of the uterus through the vagina." / "Typically, one egg matures every cycle." / "If there is no fertilization, the body sheds the uterus lining in the form of blood or blood clots" / "If the egg is fertilized, this lining of the uterus provides a home to a growing baby" / "menstruation is a normal biological process and it happens to girls when they get to puberty and ends at menopause"

Conditions: Explains the cycle only; it does not say when a girl can get pregnant, which the handbook does not state. The 28-day cycle is not stated (see NEW-G-01). Pregnancy chances (during a period, first time) need another source and clinician input.
source: Kenya MoH and MoE, MHM in Schools: A Handbook for Teachers, "Menstruation Cycle", p. 8; "Psychological Well Being", p. 21
